People are worrying:  economists,      politicians, businesspeople who know that retail sales drive our economy.      This week, the CEO of the nation's largest retailer, Wal-Mart, said      customers have put the price of gasoline at the top of their list of      concerns.  Joining us is Howard Davidowitz.  He heads the retail      consulting firm Davidowitz & Associates in Manhattan.
Howard, can we begin with this expression of concern from Wal-Mart CEO      Lee Scott.  When you read that, what did you think?

Well, I go      even beyond that.  We're energy-dependent, and when you look at what's      going on, the world's biggest oil producer, Saudi Arabia, completely      unstable, this Wahhabism and everything else.  It's hurricane season and      the US oil wells in the Gulf of Mexico may be at risk.  We have a major      energy crisis.  We've know it for 20 years.  We've done absolutely zero.      America lives in a fool's paradise.  That's our style.
Hey, you know, you're in retail consulting.  People buy what      they want to buy.

You got it, and here's how they're doing it.  They're      re--the consumer has the highest debt in the history of the United      States.  Interest rates are going up.  The consumer has no savings.  How      have we continued to spend money?  How has this consumer continued to      spend?  Here's how.  The savings finally went down to zero and they're      hocking their houses, taking second and third mortgages.  We go right on      spending.  We're the world's biggest consumers.  When you look at the      whole picture, here's what you know: We can't keep it up.
You have an analysis of what you call the Wal-Mart customer      and what the cost of energy means to this person.
Right.
It's a thousand dollars a year.  Would you explain that?

The reality of the Wal-Mart customer is when you make      $44,000 in the family of four and--between home heating oil and gas and      everything else, a thousand dollars of your disposable income goes away,      and that's the number that's gone away.  You have to understand the real      America.  We get confused.  A hundred million customers come to Wal-Mart      a week.  Twenty-five percent of them don't have bank accounts.  When they      come to the store, they have $18 in their pocket and they have to buy      food and everything else.  But you got to understand that's a large part      of America.
You said there were a hundred million people shopping at      Wal-Marts a week.  That can't be true.
A hundred million Americans.

So you're saying that a third of the country is about at their      limit, and they are the people who are trying to struggle with an      increased cost of living of a thousand dollars a year, and that's all      energy prices, and that's what's going on?

The problem is that person shopping at Wal-Mart is the      one struggling to survive.  They're in survival mode.  If you look at      where these kind of people shop, you're going to find that their      sales--and all the places they shop are under stress.  And the point is      you're taking money out of their pocket.  The mess that's been created is      beyond imagination, and the economic consequences are going to be huge.
Howard Davidowitz, chairman of the retail consulting firm      Davidowitz & Associates, speaking with us from Manhattan.  Howard, thanks      again.
Thanks for inviting me.
I'm Ferai Chideya.  This is DAY TO DAY.

It's the day after Christmas.  If you didn't get the gift you'd been      hoping for, or if you're just hungering for bargains, chances are you'll      be heading to the stores.  Today's also the day that retailers start to      take stock of their end-of-year fortunes.  Joining us now to talk about      holiday sales figures is retail analyst, Howard Davidowitz, of the      consulting firm of Davidowitz & Associates.  Welcome back to DAY TO DAY.
Thanks for inviting me.
OK, so the smoke clears and how did retailers make out this      year?

I think it'll be very mixed.  I think you'll see      department stores not do so good.  I think even discounters will be      mixed.  I don't think you're going to see Wal-Mart with very good      earnings, so I think what you have--it's an electronics holiday.  But I      don't think RadioShack and Gamestop did too well.  Even Best Buy gave an      earnings warning.  I think it's going to be a mixed picture in the retail      business.
Were there any sectors that did particularly well?

Oh, yeah.  We had some huge winners.  For example, in      electronics, you couldn't get into the Apple Store.  In apparel, I mean,      Abercrombie & Fitch absolutely fantastic.  A lot of jewelry people did      very, very well.  So we had a lot of big, big winners.  But when it's all      added up, for example--here we are finished with Christmas.  How did toys      do?  Toys did less than last year.  Not too exciting.  Actually, the      biggest category that exploded was electronics.  But again, Circuit City      did great.  Apple did great, but that was a mixed picture, too.  We had      winners and losers.
So what were some of the factors in this whole situation?      You've got the weather, the transit strike in New York City, people      feeling unsecure about the economy.

I think the biggest factor is, you know--if you take the      last quarter, household income--household spending exceeded income at the      rate of 572 billion.  That's bigger than the federal budget deficit.      Households since the late '90s have been spending more than they make.      There's no way to sustain it.  And when you add to that increased      interest rates, inflation-adjusted income down in the first time in 20      years, zero savings, the consumer really, just like the country, is in      terrible shape.  We're in a sea of debt.  We're a house of cards.  And I      think the consumers are starting to worry about it and, of course, now      you've got increased energy prices topping that off.
Howard, you're depressing me.
I'm sorry.  I didn't mean to do it.
That's OK.  So what about post-holiday sales?  Is it a      situation where these retailers are going to make up some of their money      after Christmas and after the holiday rush?

Oh, yeah.  I think this is going to be a big week and I      think today is going to be a big, big day.  A lot of people are off      today. There's going to be a lot of shopping today and a lot of people      are going to charge into the stores with those gift cards which are      exploding.  So I look for today to be a very big, important day and for      this week to be a good week. At the end, the season is still going to be      mixed, but I think this is going to be an important day and an important      week for retailers.
Finally and briefly, what about Internet sales?

Internet sales, it's the best sector in retail.  Up 25      percent.  And the exciting thing about Internet sales is the base keeps      growing, and the increase is there, which is astounding.  So this year      will do 220 billion when you include travel.  My God, increased 25      percent.  That's an incredible number.  We're addicted to online shopping      and it's exploding.
Howard Davidowitz is chairman of the retail consulting firm,      Davidowitz & Associates.  Thanks so much for joining us.
Thanks for inviting me.
DAY TO DAY returns in a moment.  I'm Ferai Chideya.
